## Study area and setting

Steamboat Hills sits a few kilometers south of Reno, Nevada, at the
northern end of a fault-bounded belt of Great Basin geothermal systems
and is one of the longest-studied hydrothermal areas in the western
United States. The system has been characterized geologically and
hydrologically since the 1950s [@thompsonwhite1964; @white1968;
@white1968c; @silberman1979], produced commercially for electricity
since the mid-1980s, and is currently operated by Ormat Technologies
as a binary, fully-reinjected geothermal field generating on the order
of 79 MW net [@dhakal2025]. Ormat's own production/injection network
is conventionally divided into three thermal zones -- Upper, Middle,
and Lower Steamboat -- reflecting a natural-state upflow of roughly
220-240 degrees Celsius beneath Upper Steamboat that cools along
northeast-striking faults toward the Middle and Lower fields
[@dhakal2025; @johnsonhulen2006].

At the surface, this deep system expresses itself through the Lower
Sinter Terrace: an area of active and historically active fumaroles,
seeps, and hot springs at the Steamboat Springs Area of Critical
Environmental Concern. This surface expression has not been static.
Sorey and Colvard [@sorey1992] documented a near-total cessation of
natural spring flow at the main and low silica terraces between 1986
and 1989, attributing most (though not all) of the decline to regional
shallow-groundwater drawdown rather than to Ormat's (then CPI/SB GEO's)
own geothermal production. Sorey [@sorey2000] revisited the same
terrace roughly a decade later and found that although regional
groundwater levels had by then recovered, natural spring flow on the
main terrace had not resumed. That non-recovery is the single most
important piece of historical context for this thesis: it establishes
that surface discharge at Steamboat is not simply a mirror of
groundwater level, and that a system which goes quiet does not
necessarily reawaken on its own.

It was against that backdrop that, beginning around 2022, steaming
ground at the Lower Sinter Terrace began to expand again, and on
June 3, 2025, an uncapped, shallow abandoned well erupted without
warning, sending boiling water roughly 30 meters into the air -- the
first geyser-like activity documented at Steamboat in decades
[@lindsey2026]. The well was capped in the following days to weeks,
but discharge did not stop; it moved laterally, opening new seeps and
spitting vents along nearby fractures. This event, and the still-open
question of what it means for the system's deeper plumbing, motivates
essentially everything in this thesis: a remapping of springs at the
Lower Sinter Terrace that Ormat's own records list as inactive, a
renewed chemistry and isotope sampling program at the wells and
springs there, a re-examination of Sorey's own chloride-discharge
method against the modern system, continuous temperature and
conductivity monitoring at the creek and at the eruption site itself,
and the geodatabase and geospatial-analysis platform, described in the
chapters that follow, built to hold all of it together.

## A brief chronology

Table 1.1 traces this study area from its first systematic USGS
characterization through the present monitoring effort; the
corresponding figure (Figure 1.1) places the same events on a single
timeline. Three broad periods are worth distinguishing. The
**historical/characterization period** (roughly 1950-1968) established
the regional geology, structure, and hydrology that every later study,
including this one, still relies on [@thompsonwhite1964; @white1968;
@white1968c]. The **development period** (1986-2007) covers the
transition from a natural system to a commercially produced one, the
1987-89 spring-flow decline documented by Sorey and Colvard
[@sorey1992], its documented non-recovery by 2000 [@sorey2000], and
the buildout of the groundwater/geothermal monitor-well network that
Klein, Johnson, and Spielman [@klein2007] describe. The **reawakening
period** (2022-present) covers the renewed steaming, the June 2025
eruption, and this project's own response.

(2026)'s own stage-by-stage detail, with Ormat's May 2025 injection-limit increase flagged (triangle) as a candidate contributing factor, not a confirmed cause (see `scripts/analysis/manuscript_figures.R`)."


| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1950 | USGS thermal-gradient and chemistry test holes (GS-1 through GS-8) drilled [@white1968]. |
| 1964 | Regional geology and structure of the Steamboat Springs area described [@thompsonwhite1964; @white1968c]. |
| 1968 | Hydrology, activity, and heat flow of the thermal system characterized in detail [@white1968]. |
| 1986 | SB GEO's first power plants begin production; commercial development of the field begins in earnest. |
| 1987-1989 | Natural hot-spring flow at the main and low silica terraces declines and ceases [@sorey1992]. |
| 1990 | Ormat consolidates Steamboat production under a single operator. |
| 1992 | Sorey and Colvard attribute most of the spring-flow decline to regional groundwater drawdown, not geothermal production [@sorey1992]. |
| 2000 | Groundwater levels recover, but natural spring flow does not resume on the main terrace [@sorey2000]. |
| 2007 | The groundwater/geothermal monitor-well network is documented in detail [@klein2007]. |
| 2022 | Steaming ground expands and water reappears along natural fractures at the Lower Sinter Terrace, the first sign of renewed activity [@lindsey2026]. |
| 2023 | Diffuse steaming measurably expands across the lower sinter terrace; no focused vents or flowing water yet [@lindsey2026]. |
| 2024 | Activity shifts from diffuse degassing to localized seeps and vents; first evidence of shallow boiling [@lindsey2026]. |
| 2025 (early) | Existing vents intensify and discharge points begin migrating along nearby fractures [@lindsey2026]. |
| 2025-05-30 | Ormat's field-wide authorized injection limit is raised from 49,500 to 55,000 gpm (NDEP UIC Temporary Permit UNEV2007204T2025-1 [@nevadadep2025uic]) -- about two weeks before the eruption; a candidate contributing factor, not yet confirmed (see below). |
| 2025 | The Lower Sinter Terrace erupts (June 3); the wellhead is capped and discharge redistributes laterally [@lindsey2026]. NBMG begins an integrated monitoring program, and this project's temperature and conductivity logger network is deployed. |
| 2026 | Lindsey et al. publish the first full account of the eruption [@lindsey2026]; spring/well remapping and chemistry/isotope sampling continue under this thesis. |

: A brief chronology of Steamboat Hills, from first characterization to the current reawakening. {#tbl-chronology}

## Candidate explanations for the reactivation

What actually drove the 2022-2025 reactivation is an open question
this thesis does not claim to resolve, but several candidate
explanations already have real, if uneven, supporting evidence on
file, and are worth stating together rather than leaving the single
injection-permit event on Figure 1.1 unexplained.

**Increased injection pressure/rate (Ormat).** The one real, dated
regulatory document on file -- NDEP UIC Temporary Permit
UNEV2007204T2025-1 [@nevadadep2025uic] -- raised the field's combined
authorized injection-rate limit from 49,500 to 55,000 gpm on May 30,
2025, about two weeks before the eruption. The timing is suggestive,
and this is flagged explicitly on Figure 1.1 as a candidate
contributing factor. It is not yet confirmed: the permit records newly
*authorized* limits, not necessarily the rate actually injected in
practice, and the same document's own reported current pressures sit
below the prior allowable ceiling at most wells, so whether real
injection pressure or rate increased *before* the eruption, rather than
only becoming newly permitted to do so, is not resolvable from this one
document alone. A real test would need a dated, well-by-well injection
pressure/rate history spanning the 2022-2025 window, which does not yet
exist in this project.

**Conduit reactivation within the existing hydrothermal system, not a
new fluid source.** This project's own 2026 poster [@irvinlindsey2026]
found that the reactivated fissure's major-ion chemistry and stable
isotopes match the hydrothermal fluid already expressed in nearby
springs and wells, and that paired temperature loggers at the terrace
show a real inverse correlation (r = -0.68) consistent with discharge
redistributing between vents within one connected flow system. Of the
explanations considered here, this one currently has the most direct
observational support.

**Regional groundwater-level recovery remobilizing existing pathways.**
Sorey [-@sorey2000] found that groundwater levels had recovered by 2000
without natural spring flow resuming, which argues that recovery alone
has historically been insufficient to reactivate this system. Whether
a slower, multi-decade continuation of that same recovery eventually
crossed some threshold by 2022 is untested with the data on hand.

**Local seismic triggering.** A real earthquake-catalog cross-check
against this project's own water-level record found no detectable,
co-located step-change at the three nearest real events (M1.5-1.6,
2025), and no catalogued earthquake at all overlapping the actual
temperature-logger deployment window. Current support for this
explanation is weak.

**Precipitation/recharge-driven.** A real, large December 2025 storm
produced a modest water-level response at one regional monitoring
well, but not at a second, nearby well with a different completion
depth, and no precipitation record exists on file for most of the
2022-2025 reactivation window. Support is mixed and incomplete, not
absent.

None of these explanations are mutually exclusive, and this thesis's
own calibration and remapping work is designed to generate the kind of
real, time-paired chemistry and discharge data that could eventually
discriminate between them -- it is not designed, on its own, to settle
the question now.

## Chloride discharge as a tracer of geothermal outflow

Michael Sorey's own framing of this system -- developed across
[@sorey1992], [@sorey2008], and [@sorey2017] -- is the conceptual
backbone of this thesis. Because chloride behaves conservatively in
this system (it is neither added nor removed by mineral reactions or
degassing on the way to discharge), the difference in chloride mass
flux between two points on Steamboat Creek can be used to estimate how
much thermal water is entering the creek between them, without needing
to locate or measure every individual spring or seep along the way.
Sorey and Spielman applied this method at two gauging sites, Rhodes
Road (SBRR) and Bella Vista (SBBV), reporting 730-1,214 gallons per
minute for 2007-08 [@sorey2008] and an average of 60 liters per second
(range 45-90 L/s) across 24 sampling events from 2008 to 2016
[@sorey2017]. This project's own poster, presented at the 2026
Geothermal Rising Conference in Houston, Texas, used the same method
and sites to estimate a post-eruption average discharge of roughly
27 L/s [@irvinlindsey2026], and Chapter 4 of this proposal extends that
calculation into a real, reproducible database query rather than a
one-off spreadsheet result.

The practical problem with the chloride-flux method has always been
that it requires discrete water samples, collected and analyzed in a
lab, at a temporal resolution most field campaigns cannot sustain for
long. This thesis's second major thread is testing whether continuous,
field-deployable specific-conductance monitoring -- already
demonstrated as a workable chloride proxy for geothermal solute flux
in Yellowstone's rivers [@mccleskey2012; @mccleskey2016] -- can do the
same job at Steamboat, letting a much sparser chloride-sampling
campaign be calibrated against a continuous conductance record rather
than trying to sample chloride itself at high frequency indefinitely.

## Thesis objectives

This proposal is organized around three questions, each revisited
explicitly in the Results and Discussion chapters once the data on
hand can actually speak to it:

1. **Has thermal-water outflow at Steamboat changed since Sorey's own
   studies, and if so, how?** This requires comparing modern chemistry
   and discharge estimates against the historical baseline Sorey and
   Colvard [@sorey1992], Sorey [@sorey2000], and Sorey and Spielman
   [@sorey2008; @sorey2017] established, using the same conservative
   tracers (chloride, and the chloride-to-boron ratio) wherever
   possible so that a real change is not confused with a change in
   method.
2. **Can continuous conductivity substitute for discrete chloride
   sampling, and at what sampling frequency does that substitution
   stop being reliable?** This is directly testable against the
   conductivity record already collected at SBRR and SBGG, and its
   answer determines how a real field-sampling budget should be spent
   (Chapter 3's sampling plan, Chapter 4's Monte Carlo result).
3. **What does the subsurface plumbing feeding the Lower Sinter
   Terrace actually look like, and can it be reconstructed well enough
   to test whether the 2025 eruption reactivated an existing conduit
   or opened something new?** This is the least resolved of the three
   questions today -- it depends on well water-level data this
   project has requested but not yet received, and on fault traces
   that have not yet been digitized -- and Chapters 3 and 5 lay out
   concretely what would need to happen for it to be answerable.

## What this proposal covers

Chapter 2 lays out the geochemical background and modeling methods
(PHREEQC, geothermometry, mixing) this thesis relies on. Chapter 3
describes how the supporting database was built, what data feed it,
how its quality is controlled, and the field and computational methods
-- temperature and conductivity logging, chemistry sampling, and the
hydrologic/geologic modeling this database is meant to support.
Chapter 4 presents the real findings produced so far. Chapter 5
discusses what those findings do and do not settle, and lays out the
remaining work. Chapter 6 is a focused, decision-facing proposal for
the calibration chloride-sampling campaign that Objective 2 above
depends on.
